title: Constrained nonlinear programming for volatility estimation with GARCH models
contribution: Recasts multivariate GARCH maximum-likelihood estimation as a constrained nonconvex NLP (determinant or LDL^T formulation with a stationarity side constraint) solved by FILTER/SNOPT on NEOS, obtaining much better likelihood/AIC/SIC values than diagonal VECH and BEKK.
problem_entry: Econometrics presents GARCH as unconstrained recursive models and restricts multivariate variants for tractability; the paper tests practical solvability of the general constrained NLP (p. 2).
key_idea: Keep the full VECH recursion as constraints, enforce H_t PSD via a determinant constraint or LDL^T with d_t >= 0, and compute H_t^{-1} eps_t through implied triangular-solve variables in AMPL (pp. 6-10).
assumptions: Normal likelihood; strict stationarity relaxed to <= and checked inactive (p. 5); only a KKT point claimed since objective and constraints are nonconvex (p. 5); A, B symmetric for tractability (p. 6).
proof_devices: n/a: convexity remarks only (sum of quasi-convex terms, difference-of-convex objective), pp. 5-6
experiments: S&P 500/FTSE/DAX daily returns, uni-, bi- and trivariate; FILTER and SNOPT on NEOS vs S-PLUS BHHH diagonal VECH and BEKK; wins on likelihood/AIC/SIC, higher bivariate MSE reported, run times caveated as not comparable (pp. 10-18).
positioning: Positions against econometrics texts and the VECH/BEKK/factor-ARCH line; claims the finance literature does not use modern optimization software (p. 2).
writing: States the contribution as an optimization-quality result, explicitly not a forecasting result (p. 3); hedges the timing comparison (p. 16).
limits_future: Forecasting accuracy left to further research (pp. 3, 16, 17); long NEOS run times (p. 16).

title: On the global minimization of the value-at-risk
contribution: Formulates scenario VaR minimization as an LPEC and derives LP upper bounds (restricted complementarity pieces), disjunctive and convex-hull LP lower bounds, and a small branch-and-cut that certifies global optimality; also proves convergence of a smoothing approximation (arXiv v1 preprint read).
problem_entry: CVaR-based VaR algorithms give no global guarantee and MPEC solvers are local; the authors refuse a routine local adaptation and target global optimality (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Bilevel LP to LPEC (4); upper bounds by fixing complementarity pieces at degenerate points or solving the NLP form; lower bounds via the substitution z^i = lambda_i x with three-way cuts and a McCormick hull; a small verification tree (pp. 3-13).
assumptions: X a compact polyhedron, finitely many positive-probability scenarios (p. 3); the smoothing result needs a singleton argmin and globally solved smoothed problems (p. 17).
proof_devices: finite union of polyhedra, so a strictly improving restricted-LP sequence ends at the optimum (Theorem 3.1, pp. 6-7)
degeneracy of the starting point is what allows the search to continue (p. 7)
validity of three-way disjunctive LP bounds (Proposition 3.3, p. 10; Corollary 3.4, p. 11)
smoothing convergence via the uniform approximation |t+ - rho_eps(t)| <= c eps and a boundedness lemma (Lemma 6.1, Proposition 6.2, pp. 16-17)
experiments: One constructed example (n = 3, k = 27): six LPs certify 4.2652; the two lower bounds are nondominating across beta; five NEOS NLP solvers on smoothed problems mostly fail, filter reaches 4.265827 (pp. 13-15, 18).
positioning: Builds on Rockafellar-Uryasev CVaR and Mangasarian's LPEC and smoothing work (dedication, p. 1); contrasts with local MPEC solvers, including the NLP approach of Fletcher and Leyffer (pp. 2, 7).
writing: Calls Theorem 3.1 mainly of theoretical interest (p. 7) and frames the example as an illustration (p. 1); the conclusion draws a lesson about needing proofs (p. 18).
limits_future: Lower bounding is problem dependent; extension to general LPECs and convex MPECs proposed; combine local MPEC methods with global branch-and-cut (p. 18).

method_links.note: MPEC/LPEC and NLP-solver base carried into risk management
the log-exp smoothing fails because the exponentials cannot be evaluated or blow up; the square-root form behaves better
the worst-case attitude appears as a demand for a global-optimality proof rather than a counterexample; the evidence base is one illustrative example

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Certify, not just solve: verify a local solver's answer with the smallest proof tree
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: an NLP/MPEC solver gives 4.2652, six LPs with complementarity-fixing cuts prove global optimality; the conclusion says robust NLP solvers still need such a proof

transferable: Build the smallest branch-and-cut tree that certifies a given candidate by fixing complementarity pieces against the incumbent (pp. 12-13).
Combine two nondominating relaxations and report on which instance each wins (pp. 12, 15).
Let the modelling-language presolve discard infeasible children and count only the LPs actually solved (p. 15).

quotes.text: this is one of the rare instances in mathematical programming where degeneracy actually helps: it enables one to continue the search for an improvement in a global optimization procedure.
while the NLP solvers are generally very robust, one still requires a proof such as the one given in Subsection 5.2 to ascertain the quality of the solutions they produce.

title: Biomolecule electrostatic optimization with an implicit Hessian
contribution: Improves a Hessian-implicit primal-dual interior-point method for ligand charge optimization (adaptive centering rule, equality-constrained preconditioner) and implements it at full scale with pFFT++ and PETSc, about twice as fast as the original formulation.
problem_entry: Optimal ligand charges solve a convex QP whose Hessian needs an expensive boundary-element solve per column (p. 1).
key_idea: Solve the Newton system as an expanded system containing the integral operators, never forming the Hessian, with block-diagonal preconditioning; adaptive sigma rule from the previous step length (pp. 2-3).
assumptions: Continuum electrostatics under stated assumptions gives a convex QP with PSD L; box and sum-of-charge constraints (pp. 1-2).
proof_devices: n/a: the sigma schedule is set by practical experience (p. 2)
experiments: Cost counted in M2 matrix-vector products; old vs new formulation, explicit Hessian, KNITRO (estimated cost); accuracy on chorismate mutase vs explicit Hessian (pp. 3-4).
positioning: Extends the group's earlier MSM 2003 method [4]; uses Wright's primal-dual interior-point framework (pp. 1-2).
writing: Short proceedings style; result stated as roughly a factor-of-two improvement (p. 4).
limits_future: Numerical Hessian asymmetry cannot be removed in the implicit method; future work on the asymmetry, convex constraints and constraint updates (pp. 3-4).

method_links.note: the fair unit is stated (M2 products) but the KNITRO baseline is only estimated

title: A trust-region algorithm for global optimization
contribution: Embeds the ALSO Gaussian-smoothing two-phase global method in an adaptive trust-region framework with a global-quality model-improvement test, using up to 20 times fewer local searches than ALSO and reducing sensitivity to the initial radius (preprint ANL/MCS-P1190-0804 read).
problem_entry: ALSO smooths the local-minimization map L(x) in a ball of fixed radius whose value is not clear a priori (pp. 2, 6).
key_idea: Reinterpret ALSO's radius as a trust-region radius updated by the actual/predicted reduction ratio; a global-quality measure q triggers sample discarding and region enlargement instead of shrinking (pp. 3, 8-10).
assumptions: Smooth f on a simple box; funnel structure; the cited unimodality theorem is one-dimensional and of limited usefulness (pp. 1, 3, 5).
proof_devices: n/a: no convergence theory; sigma = Delta/K^(1/n) from a volume-coverage argument (p. 8)
experiments: Rastrigin, Levy, Ackley, Schwefel, scaled Rastrigin; 1000 random trials per test; MBH, adaptive MBH and ALSO at radii optimal for MBH; success percentage and local searches per success (infinity for none); performance profiles (pp. 10-14, 17-19).
positioning: Builds on Addis-Locatelli-Schoen ALSO; contrasts with filtering f directly (More-Wu, Shao et al.) and with monotonic basin hopping (pp. 2-3, 6).
writing: Two contributions listed explicitly (p. 3); losses to AMBH acknowledged with reasons (p. 12).
limits_future: AMBH is better on Ackley and Levy; a nonmonotone version is in progress (p. 12); several TRF success rates fall below ALSO in the tables (pp. 17, 19).

method_links.note: trust-region globalization from local NLP carried into stochastic global optimization
baselines given their best radii, failures kept as infinity in the statistics, losses to AMBH stated

title: A globally convergent filter method for MPECs
contribution: Proposes an SLPEC(-EQP) filter method that keeps complementarity as structure, solves an LPEC in a trust region (d = 0 iff B-stationary) and an EQP for speed, and proves global convergence to B-stationary points under MPEC-MFCQ; small examples show that A-, C-, M-stationarity, NLP approaches and SQPEC can stall at spurious points.
problem_entry: NLP approaches to MPECs, including his own, can converge to spurious stationary points, observed on PJM electricity-market problems; A/C/M-stationarity allow trivial descent directions (pp. 3, 5).
key_idea: Complementarity as a structural constraint: the LPEC step uses the correct tangent cone and estimates the active set, an EQP accelerates, and a three-dimensional filter separates general and complementarity infeasibility (pp. 4, 9-11).
assumptions: Compact iterates, C2 data, MPEC-MFCQ at limit points (no MPEC-LICQ), and an LPEC solver that explores all eps-active partitions (Assumptions 4.1-4.4, pp. 15-16).
proof_devices: two-variable examples with C- and A/M-stationary points that admit descent directions (pp. 6-7)
closed-form SQPEC iterate recursion converging quadratically to a spurious M-stationary point, with a hypothesis check against Scholtes' local result (Proposition 2.1, p. 8)
Chin-Fletcher filter-SLP convergence pattern: LPEC bound lemma, f-type step near a nonstationary feasible point, finite inner loop, feasible limit, case split on h-type steps (Theorem 4.1, pp. 16-21)
filter margin proportional to the total violation so that limits of a 3D filter are feasible (p. 11)
experiments: none (computational cost discussed in words, pp. 22-23)
positioning: Extends Fletcher-de la Maza SLP-EQP and the Chin-Fletcher filter-SLP; criticizes the stationarity zoo surveyed by Scheel-Scholtes and Scholtes' SQPEC (pp. 4-8).
writing: Strong wording (useless, doomed) backed by small worked examples; contribution sentence on p. 4; hedged with 'To our knowledge' (pp. 5, 7-8, 10).
limits_future: Only a linear rate without EQP; worst case 2^d LP pieces per iteration; restoration failure not excluded; penalty, star-shaped and vanishing-constraint extensions (pp. 16, 21-23).

title: A filter active-set trust-region method
contribution: Proposes FASTr: active-set prediction by a regularized LP (whose dual is a bound-constrained QP) plus EQP steps under a filter, with global convergence to Fritz-John points, active-set identification near regular solutions, and equivalence of the regularization parameter to an l2 trust-region radius; no implementation yet.
problem_entry: Pivoting LP/QP subproblems and polyhedral trust regions do not scale or warm-start well; MINLP warm starts and PDE iterative solvers motivate active-set methods (pp. 3-4, 6).
key_idea: Replace TR(x, rho) by RLP: min mu g'd + 1/2 d'd, whose dual is a BQP for projected-gradient solvers; mu acts as the trust-region parameter, adjusted by a breakpoint ratio test; EQP for speed; filter globalization (pp. 7-11).
assumptions: C2 functions and iterates in a compact region (A1, A2, p. 14); LICQ and strict complementarity for active-set identification (p. 21).
proof_devices: piecewise-linear RLP solution path in mu with finitely many breakpoints (Lemma 3.2, p. 15; Corollary 3.3, p. 17)
finite inner loop and a Cauchy-step argument for EQP steps (Lemmas 3.5 and 3.8, pp. 18-19)
four-outcome global convergence to a Fritz-John point (Theorem 3.9, p. 19)
mu-interval for active-set identification from primal and dual feasibility bounds (Proposition 4.1, pp. 21-22)
RLP vs l2 trust-region LP equivalence by comparing KKT systems (Lemma 4.2, p. 23)
experiments: none; the authors say only thorough numerical experiments can justify the method's name (p. 12)
positioning: Builds on SLQP methods (Fletcher-de la Maza, Byrd-Gould-Nocedal-Waltz, Chin-Fletcher); distinguishes itself from Yamashita-Dan (pp. 5, 8).
writing: Lists open questions right after the outline (p. 4); performance claims withheld pending experiments (pp. 12, 24).
limits_future: No implementation; a preconditioner for the BQP and the ordering for iterative solvers are open questions (p. 24).

title: A Filter Active-Set Trust-Region (FASTr) Framework
contribution: Documents FASTr, a C filter trust-region SQP framework built on BQPD with a nonmonotone (shadow) filter, a restoration phase that reuses the same code with a second filter, an AMPL interface, and a 14-code termination table.
problem_entry: Need for a flexible SQP framework that admits a range of subproblem solvers (p. 3).
key_idea: l-infinity trust-region QP solved by BQPD; nonmonotone filter acceptance with memory M; switching sufficient-reduction condition; restoration via the same loop with an (h_J, h_Jperp) filter (pp. 6-9).
assumptions: Smooth C2 NLP; linear constraints consistent, checked at the start; infeasibility reported as a local minimum of the violation (pp. 3-4).
experiments: none; one sample run log on a 2-variable problem (p. 13)
positioning: Cites the Fletcher-Leyffer filter papers and the Chin-Fletcher sloping envelope (pp. 6-7, 15).
writing: Manual style; parameter defaults, output columns and termination codes documented in tables (pp. 12-14).
limits_future: Planned: hooks to other QP solvers, SLP-EQP steps, COIN-OR/CUTEr/AD interfaces (p. 15).

method_links.note: own framework with a solver API for swappable subproblem solvers; restoration reuses the same code
termination codes interpret the solver's numbers: ifail = 4 indicates CQ failure, ifail = 5 frequently means wrong gradients
explicit failure taxonomy separating normal outcomes, algorithmic failures and user-function failures
